en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the Viśvāmitra-smṛti;
here is the first chapter.
A description of the obligatory and occasional rites:
In a thousand-petaled lotus possessing the luster of the full moon, [is the deity] whose lotus-hands grant boons and fearlessness, and who is adorned with pure fragrant flowers and garments.

One should first meditate upon the Guru, who is the embodiment of all deities, whose face and eyes are serene, and who is purifying, located upon the crown of the head; this constitutes the daily observance (āhnika).
A muhūrta known as "Brahman" measures four or five ghaṭīs;
the time of dawn (uṣaḥkāla) is considered to consist of five times five ghaṭīs. The period known as "aruṇodaya" (the break of dawn) measures six ghaṭīs.
The period of five *ghaṭikās* from dawn is known as the morning (*prātaḥkāla*).
Having understood this, one should perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*) at dawn;
for when the daily, occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites are performed at their proper time, they yield excellent fruit.

Rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having performed purification with a concentrated mind, one should perform the bath at dawn for one's own sake when the sun is about to rise. In the morning, one should perform the recitation (*japa*); this is known as the obligatory and occasional duty.
Having observed the sun when it possesses its rays, one should perform the ritual service (*upasthāna*).
There is a fault in transgressing the primary time for the *saṃdhyā* prayer;
that which has passed its time should not be performed, but that which is joined with the proper time must be performed.

Therefore, with every effort, one should perform one's duties at the proper time. If, however, through negligence, a duty is not performed at the time prescribed, one should perform three thousand recitations; this is ordained as the expiation.
Thus it has been taught regarding the two or three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Alternatively, one incurs fault by exceeding the time limit for mere recitation;
[the number of repetitions] should be three thousand, or a thousand, or three hundred, or even just a hundred.
By reciting [the mantra] in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, the destruction of sins occurs;
however, if the prescribed time has elapsed, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) serves as the authority.
One should perform a thousand recitations in both direct and reverse order.
Even for one who possesses physical well-being and a healthy mind,
if time is constantly wasted, his sin is not reckoned;
having fallen away from all paths, he shall attain the state of an animal.
Merely by seeing him, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. Those who pass their time in idle chatter, in evil company, or even in sleep, are killers of Brahman.
He who performs all the daily rites at the prescribed times shall conquer all worlds and, in the end, go to the city of Viṣṇu;
having risen every morning and completed his bath and the twilight prayers (sandhyā).
The wise man should recite [the mantra] according to his capacity; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born one, knowing that the last watch of the night consists of five *nāḍīs*, he should perform his daily rites at that time, which is known as the morning.
The time for the rite is at the end of the day, three ghaṭīs less one quarter (3.75 ghaṭīs).

Having seen the [sun's] disc, one should offer the arghya and cease; one should recite [the mantra] until the rising of the stars, once the six observances have been completed according to their respective mantras.
The man who performs his daily obligatory rites shall attain success in his actions;
however, an action performed at an improper time is fruitless,
just as rain falling out of season upon the earth.
Untimely rain renders sown seeds fruitless, making the labor performed go to waste.
But actions performed at the appointed time yield immediate success and happiness, just as seeds sown produce fruits in due season; for rain upon the earth is the very life of all things.
The definition of the three junctions (sandhyās) is as follows:
the morning twilight is considered to be of three kinds—the best is accompanied by stars, the middling has its stars obscured, and the lowest is joined with the sun. 22

The highest [period] is that of the morning sun, the middling is that of the midday sun, and the lowest is that of the western sun; thus the midday junction (madhyasandhyā) is considered to be threefold.
The highest is accompanied by the sun, while the middling has its light eclipsed by the sun.
The evening twilight is considered to be of three types, the lowest being that which is accompanied by stars.
Whether pure or impure, one should never abandon the daily obligatory rite (*nityakarman*);
even therein, the offering of the *arghya* water is distinguished by its specific timing.
At the three junctions of the day, a twice-born man, facing either the east or the north, should perform the threefold pure *ācamana*;
he should never do so facing the south or the west.
(26) He who neglects the twilight bath (*sandhyā-snāna*) and engages in the study of knowledge [is at fault].
His knowledge shall perish, and unrighteousness will certainly ensue.
(27) One should perform the ritual bath and the twilight prayers according to the method of the teacher’s instruction;
this is the means for attaining the perfection of knowledge regarding all sciences, beginning with the Vedas. (28)
Thus is the sequential rule for the study of knowledge by the twice-born castes;
he who studies knowledge otherwise does not achieve success in that knowledge.
That evil-minded person who neglects the *sandhyā* when its time has arrived—
One incurs the sin of killing an embryo and is reborn in the womb of a crow.
One should perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) according to one's ability; at the proper time of day, one obtains the full fruit.
Therefore, one should diligently perform the daily rites (nityakarman) at their appointed times.
Conduct is said to be of two kinds: that with attributes (*sopādhi*) and that without attributes (*anupādhika*).
That which is with attributes consists merely of qualities (*guṇa*), while the primary conduct is that which is without attributes.
When an attribute has been encountered, one should practice the conduct associated with it.
And he who, out of evil intellect, practices figurative conduct toward one who is free from limiting adjuncts,
shall incur poverty, great disease shall arise for him, and great censure— a grave defect— shall occur birth after birth. (33–34)
He who abandons the primary conduct and practices secondary conduct has undoubtedly conquered neither his actions nor his virtues;
for primary conduct is great, excellent, and the means for attaining liberation for one seeking release.
At the appropriate time, the twice-born should perform the primary conduct as prescribed (36).
He should thus worship his own guru with the five types of service and true devotion; this *Saṃhitā* was composed by Viśvāmitra (37).
The Brahmin who, having risen at dawn, awakens Kuṇḍalinī residing at the root of his own self, should meditate there upon Gāyatrī when it is truly morning—
Gāyatrī, who has arisen from Kuṇḍalinī and sustains the vital breaths. 38.138-139a.
The science of breath (*prāṇavidyā*) is the great science; he who knows it is a knower of Yoga.
Kuṇḍalinī is to be known as eightfold, according to the number of the thirty-two syllables.
Having understood this, one should likewise place [the syllables] in the six centers (*ṣaḍādhāra*) when dawn has broken.
One should place the six-breasted [mantra] consisting of four syllables within the six foundations;
one should place the six-breasted [mantra] in sequence, joined with the initial Praṇava.
Residing in the middle of the thousand-petaled [lotus], she is endowed with fruit and possesses the fourth vowel.
Thus, I am to be known as "Haṃsa," preceded by the knowledge of its conceptualization (42).
By the mere conceptualization of this, one is liberated from all sins;
there is no knowledge equal to this, and no recitation equal to this (43).
O Goddess whose garment is the ocean and whose breasts are the mountains, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a knowledge equal to this.
O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive my touch of your feet.
"O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon!
Homage to you, Bhairava; you should grant me permission.
Then, having risen and gone outside, the twice-born man should void his excrement, urine, and so forth. 45–46.

Let all the deities— the regions, the sages, the lords of the hosts, and the yogins— depart from the southern direction of the village for a distance of one hundred *dhanus*; here I perform my purification.
First is the binding of the head, and second is the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder (nivīta).
The third is the surveying of the directions, and the fourth is concealment. Silence is to be known as the fifth, and excretion is indeed the sixth. 48.
The seventh is the application of earth, and water is recorded as the eighth.
Having taken a handful of grass, one should perform the act of purification with a concentrated mind, facing south at night and facing north during the day. 49–50.

The best of the twice-born should wear the sacred thread over the left ear and under the right arm, and he should perform purification after voiding urine and excrement according to the path prescribed by the rules, using water drawn from a source. 51. He should act according to the method stated in the injunctions.

He who performs purification with water from wells, streams, ponds, and the like, does not return from hell even after hundreds of millions of kalpas. [One should apply earth] once on the penis, three times on the hands, and likewise five times on the anus. (52–53)

The number four is prescribed for the two feet; this is the purification ordained for the householder, while for others it is distinct. One should perform double the purification prescribed by the Smṛtis, and likewise, a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) should perform triple.
For ascetics, it is fourfold; for the three [other orders], there is the distinction of *īrati*.
Having performed purification until the removal of foul odors with a concentrated mind, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth.
The elder brother should use *kṣīrakāṣṭha* wood for cleaning his teeth;

however, he may always use grass or leaves, except on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*). On those two days as well, he may use *jambū*, *plakṣa*, *amlapana*, or *kaṇaka* wood.
"O Lord of the Forest, grant us longevity, strength, fame, speech, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence;
[and likewise] spittle and mouthfuls of water," [reciting this], a man facing the northwest direction— 58–59.
Facing the northeast, one should cast it out at the end of the northwest;
nor should one perform the cleaning of teeth with charcoal, sand, ashes, fingernails, bricks, clods of earth, or stones.

The *svadira*, the *karañja*, the *kadamba*, and likewise the *vaṭa*; the *veṇu*, the *tintiḍī*, and the *plakṣa*, as well as the *āmra* and the *nimba*; the *apāmārga*, the *bilva*, the *arka*, and likewise the *audumbara*. (61–62)
These are declared to be recommended for the act of cleaning the teeth;
one should perform the cleaning of the teeth according to one's ability. Then, having approached a river while preceded by meditation upon the Gaṅgā.

One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra, or perform it three times; having taken water in the left hand, it should be consecrated three times with the Vyāhṛtis. 64
Having drawn [the breath] into the right side, one should exhale through the left path;
looking toward one's own left side, one should release it from the vajra-stone.
Then, having sipped pure water again, one should perform the ritual bath.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should perform the bath three times;
this constitutes the different types of baths.
One should then perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma) accompanied by ten recitations of the Praṇava.
One should draw the diagram for purification (mārjana-yantra) and thoroughly draw the diagram for bathing (snāna-yantra).
Having invoked [the deity] over the water with the Gaṅgā-mantra using the appropriate mudrā,
one should draw the circle of fire (vahnimaṇḍala) together with the nasal bindu in the midst of the water.
Having clearly pronounced the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīm), [one should recite] the three Vyāhṛtis over the staffs;
then, having sipped pure water and likewise performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
one should announce the place and time, preceded by meditation on the Gāyatrī.
One should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the *sūkta* according to the path prescribed in the scriptures (70).
One should bathe while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra, preceded by the five-limbed rite (*pañcāṅga*). [The five limbs are:
the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), the recitation of the *sūkta*, the sprinkling (*mārjana*), and the *aghamarṣaṇa* (71).
The libation to the gods and others, and the fivefold bath characterized by [the following]:
bathing the head, bathing the neck, and likewise bathing the waist;
and the bath up to the knees and down to the feet—thus the mantra-bath is fourfold. (72)
Sprinkling the head with the eight syllables beginning with *ta*,
one should perform the bathing of the throat with the eight syllables beginning with *bha*,
and the bathing of the waist with the eight syllables beginning with *sa*.
One should perform [the ritual] with the eight syllables beginning with *pa* on the knees and the feet;
by this mere knowledge alone, one obtains the fruit of bathing a hundred times in the Gaṅgā. (75) A Brahmin who performs a water-bath without the mantra-bath [obtains no such fruit].
Indeed, his mind lacks the purity enjoined by the Vedas.
Having bound his ears, nose, and eyes, he should suddenly plunge into the water and remain submerged,
reciting the mantra until the breath is completely restrained.
Then one should perform the threefold bath preceded by the *śiras* mantra and the *vyāhṛtis*;
at the three times of day, one should bathe in the three ways— using water, earth, and [mantras]—
which is declared by the wise as the "five-moistures" (*pañcārdraka*) performed sequentially at the three locations.
O best of the twice-born, one should sprinkle the head and body twelve times with the conch-mudrā; then, using the mantra beginning with the *vyāhṛtis* and ending with the *Śiras*,
one should perform it six times at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and three times on each of the two arms.
One should worship the root mantra mentally with five offerings;
for the sake of satisfying the Brahman-sages and the ancestors, one should perform the libation three or four times,
using the *vyāhṛtis* joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and ending with "namaḥ."
One should offer libations with those respective mantras, accompanied by the fourth [syllable] and joined with the three worlds.
He who bathes in water without performing the libation becomes like a fish;
therefore, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rules with every effort.
"Whatever water has been defiled by me through the removal of bodily impurities— for the sake of purifying that sin, I offer libations to Yakṣman.
Having thus offered three handfuls of water outside, which is pleasing to Yakṣman—
Then, having reached the bank, one should recite the Gāyatrī-kavaca. Indeed,
the ten qualities produced by bathing for a man are beauty, splendor, strength, purity,
longevity, health, freedom from greed, the destruction of bad dreams, austerity, and intelligence.
When a Brahmin sets out for the purpose of bathing, the gods along with the hosts of ancestors approach him, afflicted by thirst; if he does not bathe, he shall go to hell.
At midday, one should always perform a bath with clay, free from sloth.

One should not perform the application of clay at the time of morning or evening. Likewise, one should not wear garments that are stitched with thread, nor those that are frayed, nor those that are variegated.
One should not wear garments made of various dolls or other types of cloth;
all such items have been described thus. However, silk garments (paṭṭavastra) are not subject to this fault, and a wise person may wear all kinds of woolen garments (aurṇavastra) without any defect.
Bathing in the morning and at midday is prescribed for forest-dwellers and householders; for ascetics, bathing occurs three times a day, while for celibate students it is performed repeatedly.
Having sprinkled [the body] and donned the garment with the six-syllable mantra beginning with the *praṇava*, [one should proceed].
One should take a pure, washed cloth that conforms to the rule of six fringes (kaccha).
Two fringes should be at the middle of the cloth, and four at its two ends; in this manner one should tie it according to the characteristics prescribed by the Vedas. 92–93.
Having washed the remnants of his meal, the best of the twice-born should perform the evening *saṃdhyā*; otherwise, he becomes a slayer of Brahman.
Having bathed in the morning and at midday, he should likewise perform the respective *saṃdhyā* prayers.

This is the duty of a householder; indeed, for yogis, it is precisely at dawn that the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and the retention of vital air (vāyudhāraṇa) is most highly recommended for yogis during the hour of dawn.
Then, having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra and stayed there for three Brahma-days,
a twice-born man who restrains his breath obtains that same fruit;
even there, he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) by practicing the kumbhaka.
Starting from sunrise, after twelve ghaṭikās have passed (97),
one should perform the bath that is an auxiliary to the Brahma-yajña; in the afternoon,
however, one should offer libations and perform the Brahma-yajña according to one's capacity after making the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) (98).
One should perform the midday rite and likewise offer libations at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*).
A water-bath devoid of the *yantra*, a *yantra* devoid of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), or a seed-syllable devoid of the nasal drop (*bindu*)—such a bath is in vain; of this there is no doubt. (99)
One who is devoid of mantra, having bathed in water, should perform the *sandhyā-vandana*;
yet for one whose mind is impure, that [bath] does not lead to purity at all.
If one performs bathing and *sandhyā* while being devoid of mantra and the ritual framework (*yantra*), [it is ineffective]. 100–101.
The power of the mantra will be fruitless—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt—if one performs the evening *saṃdhyā* without the fivefold ablution (*pañcasnāna*).
His sin will not depart, just as darkness does not leave when the sun has set. 102.
Having put on a beautiful garment, one should then apply a *tilaka*. The application of the *puṇḍra* must follow the path of the Guru’s instruction; otherwise, it is a destroyer of dharma.
One should place soft water, sandalwood, and ashes in the left hand.

Having drawn a triangular yantra, one should write the *māyā* (hrīṃ) with its bindu in the center; the *praṇava* (oṃ) should be written at the tips of the corners, and the three *vyāhṛtis* on the sides. 104–105.

Having consecrated it with the Gāyatrī, the king of mantras, one should apply a tilaka on the forehead up to ten times, preceded by the worship of the Guru. (107) If one should wear a tilaka that is devoid of mantra and yantra, [it is ineffective].
That face appears like a corpse; the splendor of Brahman is not found there.
(108) Wherever a *tilaka* is applied, and specifically one joined with mantras, is seen upon the forehead, that is the splendor named Brahman. (109)
He on whose forehead the *praṇava*, the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*), the three steps (*tripadā*), and the triple mark (*tripuṇḍraka*) are seen shall become radiant and a bestower of Brahman.
One should perform the binding of the topknot with the mantra "Oṃ āpaḥ jyotiḥ."
One should perform the twilight worship (sandhyāvandana) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own scriptures;
otherwise, he who performs it differently shall attain an asuric body.
When I have voided urine or feces, I shall perform the purification, washing, gargling, and cleansing of the private parts.
And for the washing of my garment, O Gaṅgā, be well-pleased and forgive my transgression.

(112) One should write the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center of the triangle and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the tips of the corners; likewise, one should inscribe the *vyāhṛtis* upon the staffs in the water. (113)
Having encircled [the water] with the *praṇava* (Om) and drunk the water, one should then perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*).
One should likewise perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*) by means of this [mantra]; otherwise, it becomes like that of a *śūdra*.
114. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Application of the Daily Ritual Rules," in the *Śrī Viśvāmitra Saṃhitā*.
Now begins the second chapter:
A Description of the Rules for Ācamana (Ritual Sipping of Water).
Having placed the left hand within the water like the right ear, [one should perform the rite].

Having first paid homage to the Guru, one should thereafter perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). If one sips water facing east, it becomes nectar; facing north, one becomes a drinker of Soma;
facing west, one becomes a drinker of blood; and facing south, one becomes a drinker of liquor.
One should touch the respective limbs while reciting the twenty-four names; one should install Keśava and the others, which constitutes the Puranic sipping of water (ācamana).
This is done with the twenty-four syllables beginning with *ta* and ending with *ya*.
One should touch those respective limbs and perform the Smārta ācamana (ritual sipping of water).
Having performed ācamana three times with the feet of the Goddess, one should touch [the body] with the nine *abliṅga* mantras,
the seven *vyāhṛtis*, the *gāyatrī*, and the *śiras* as the fourth, according to that tradition.

Rinsing the mouth (ācamana) is declared to be threefold— Paurāṇa, Smārta, Āgamika, Śrauta, and Mānasa— and is further said to be fivefold. One should perform these three types of rinsing at the commencement times of the Sandhyā prayers.
One should drink water at the *brahmatīrtha* with the fingers drawn together;
with the thumb and little finger released, the remainder of the hand shall be used for *ācamana*.
With the hand shaped like a cow’s ear, one should drink water in the measure of a *māṣa*.
That water, by being merely deficient or excessive, becomes equal to liquor;

therefore, one should perform the ceremonial sipping (ācamana) with mantras in due order at the beginning and at the end. One should recite the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas in regular succession and in reverse order.
With the three fingers joined and the thumb and little finger released, they say the shape is like a cow's ear; this is proclaimed as the Brāhma-karman.
One should not discard the water remaining after drinking that which was held in the middle of the hand.
In some cases one should perform renunciation, and in others drinking; they know such a person to be a wicked Brāhmaṇa.
One should drink water, black gram, and curd in sequence with the three [mantras] beginning with Keśava.
Having placed Govinda in front, and Viṣṇu specifically in the *sauṣumna* [channel].
One should place Madhusūdana in the sun and Trivikrama in the moon;
Vāmana in front, Śrīdhara likewise in the two hands, and Hṛṣīkeśa and Padmanābha on both feet. 13–14.
One should place Dāmodara in the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*), and likewise, one should assign the name Saṃkarṣaṇa either in the middle of the nose or at its tip;
and in the same manner, one should place Vāsudeva in the right nostril.
One should assign Pradyumna to the left [side] and Aniruddha to the right (16). One should assign Puruṣottama to the left eye, Adhokṣaja to the right ear,
Nārasiṃha to the left ear, and Acyuta to the navel (17).

Having placed Janārdana in the heart, one should place Upendra at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); and one should place Hari and Kṛṣṇa on the right and left arms respectively. This [system], consisting of the Paurāṇa and Smārta traditions, is prescribed for Kṣatriyas. 18–19.
O lover of hymns, may these songs encompass you from every side;
may they be increasing for you who are already grown, and may the pleasing offerings be well-received.
(20) Likewise, it should be known that for virtuous women and Śūdras, there is only the mere mention of their names.
One should perform the threefold mode of pure sipping of water during all rites at the three junctions of the day;
the commencement should be joined with the name Keśava.
Thus it is said to be twofold according to the Śruti and Smṛti.
Having taken water with the Devatīrtha, one should drink it at the Brahmatīrtha;
[the manner] with the thumb and little finger released is called the "cow-ear" (gokarṇa) shape. 21–22.

Therefore, at the beginning of all activities, one should always perform the prescribed rites with self-restraint during the three periods of the day, following the path of the Purāṇas as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti; hence, the pure *ācamana* is preeminent.
Furthermore, one should utter "Oṃ" at the beginning of names, at the beginning of syllables, and at the beginning of verses.
One should place the mantra ending with "namaḥ" and "oṃ"; thus purified, it becomes threefold.
(24) There are twenty-four feet, twenty-four syllables, and twenty-four names, beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*. (25)

For Vaiśyas, however, [the mantra] should end with "namaḥ"; for others, it should consist of the name alone; for virtuous women, it should end with "namaḥ," especially in the case of [mantras] such as Keśava and the rest. For Śūdras and widows, the water-rite consists of the name alone.
And having performed the ritual sipping (ācamana) twice with the name [of the deity] ending in "namaḥ" while facing a maiden, one becomes purified.
(27) The threefold ending in "namaḥ" and likewise the threefold Praṇava should be known;
in this very manner, having performed the ritual sipping three times, one should perform that at the beginning of any rite. (28)
Otherwise, the *ācamana* performed is indeed fruitless;
it should be accompanied by the full five-fingered hand-mudrā and the recitation of [mantras] beginning with "Keśava," during spitting,
falling asleep, putting on a garment, and the shedding of tears.

One should sip water at the five openings [of the head], or else touch the right ear; at the beginning and end of a meal, one should always consume water in the manner of a cow’s ear with the hand, otherwise it is not accompanied by *darbha* grass. 29–30.
While reciting the three *vyāhṛtis* over the nostrils, eyes, and ears, one should touch the ears and the measure of the breath; thus it is enjoined by the Śruti.
One should mentally contemplate the *praṇava* as joined with the short, long, and protracted [vowels].
One should perform the mental sipping of water (mānasācamana) according to the sequence of the mental procedure.
Having drunk water with three feet [of the mantra], one should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) by placing [water] with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā. 32.
Grant us strength and exhilaration for our delight;
O Soma, of that which is most auspicious for you, grant us a share from the very beginning.
May I place within my hands those yearning [powers] and wear them upon my breast.
For the destruction of whomsoever, you two indeed generate the head from the left;
having placed the foot of *bhūḥ* at the end of the nose, the foot of *bhuvaḥ* on the right side, the foot of *suvaḥ* on the left part, and the foot of *mahaḥ* on the right. (34-35)
One should place the *jana* foot on the left eye, the *tapaḥ* foot on the right,
the *satya* foot on the left hand, and the first foot of the Goddess on the navel (36). One should place the second [foot] on the heart and the third on the *brahmarandhra*.
One should place *kha*, *āpaḥ*, and *jyotiḥ* on the right arm (37),
and one should place the fourth quarter on the left arm in the sequence prescribed by the Vedas;
that best of the twice-born who performs the sipping of water for Hari with these [mantras] (38).

He shall be liberated from all sins; there is no distinction between what is touched and what is untouched. The three feet, the nine words, and likewise the seven worlds, followed again by the three feet and the head—the fourth—is declared to be the Śrauta.

The fourth foot is the head, and together with the three-footed Gāyatrī and the seven vyāhṛtis, there are nine feet and three quarters; one should not assign these twenty-four feet to those [other] locations. 40–41.
It is taught that there are three [syllables] at the beginning, nine, sevenfold, three, and two *śrutis*.
Having formed the *gāyatrī*, one should touch with the nine [verses] beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*;
and likewise, one should touch with the seven *vyāhṛtis* and the three feet of the *gāyatrī*.
One should touch the head with the foot while reciting the twenty-four [syllables].
This is indeed known as the *śrutya-ācamana* by Viśvāmitra and others; it consists of the name, the syllable, the quarter-verse, and the words *bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*. 43–44.
These five sips of water (pañcācamana) have been proclaimed by the hosts of the Svacchandatantra;
with the three vyāhṛtis, one should then touch the head, the eyes, the two nostrils, and the ears, as well as the heart, with water.
"One should sip water three times," "one should rub [the lips] three times," and "one should touch [the lips] once"— thus has it been enjoined by the Śruti. 46.
During the *brahmayajña*, one should sip water three times according to the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*;
it should be understood that there are two [sips] for wiping here, and one should cleanse the palate with the hand.
One should touch the water once with the thumb while reciting the *praṇava*.
Any other [water] touched by a stream would make that ritual act fruitless.
[One should perform] twenty-four foot-washes, twenty-four applications of unguents, and twenty-four recitations of names; one should sip water three times according to the rule. 48–49.
Likewise, having wiped [the mouth] twice, one should touch the moon and the sun—the two *svaras*—and also touch the *suṣumnā*; this is done once by people during the *brahmayajña*.
During the *brahmayajña*, one should sip water three times; [this applies to] the Śrauta, Smārta, and Paurāṇika rites.

Having wiped [the teeth] three times with the hand, one should touch the principal limb [of the body] and recite the *praṇava* once while wiping. [This applies] during eating, at home, in giving, bathing, and in receiving gifts. 51–52.
One should perform the preliminary sipping of water (ācamana) five times after sleeping during the three junctions of the day, as well as when putting on a garment and upon entering a street;
first one should perform the Vedic (śrauta) sipping, and then the traditional (smārta) sipping.
Therefore, the Purāṇic [method] is prescribed for the daily ācamana and for the Śrāddha;
at the time of the Śrāddha, the Purāṇic is used, and at the conclusion of the Śrāddha, the Smārta is said to be used.
For the Pārvaṇa rite, the Śrauta method applies to the ācamana, while the placement (nyāsa) in the Śrāddha is performed in reverse order.
During the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) and the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should perform [the recitation] with the root mantra alone.

One must avoid giving what is difficult to give, accepting what is difficult to accept, eating forbidden food, wicked speech, engaging in idle chatter and the like, and association with wicked women. 56.

"By merely performing the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the prescribed rule, one instantly removes everything, including contact with those of the Cāṇḍāla caste and all that causes defilement.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Application of Pure Ācamana," in the Viśvāmitra Smṛti.
Now begins the third chapter:
A Description of the Rules for Prāṇāyāma;
Prāṇāyāma.
One should place meditation equally within the bodies of all embodied beings;
therein, one should also place breath control (prāṇāyāma) equally for those of the twice-born castes. One should perform three rounds of breath control at the time of the morning twilight ritual.
The union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is known as prāṇāyāma. It is said that the highest form is ninefold, while the middling is sixfold;
this is declared to be the characteristic of prāṇāyāma when accompanied by mantras.
Prāṇāyāma is prescribed with the seven vyāhṛtis preceded by the praṇava in their proper order, together with the Gāyatrī and its Śiras;
it is the unification of the Bindu, the Prāṇa, and the Visarga, being the Gāyatra joined with the Bindu.
Likewise, during breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should touch [the body] while joined with the *śiras* and the *vyāhṛtis*.
First, having resorted to *kumbhaka* devoid of exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), one should perform the breath control beginning with the *vyāhṛtis* and ending with the *śiras*.
In obligatory, occasional, and optional rites— at all times and in all actions—
one should perform exhalation and inhalation by relying first upon *kumbhaka* (retention).
This applies likewise at the time of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), at the time of fire offerings (*homa*), and during the Vedic study sacrifice (*brahmayajña*).
First, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma), which is to be understood through the kumbhaka [retention];

it is joined with the three locks (bandhas) along with prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and bindu, and is further characterized by the seven vyāhṛtis, the encapsulation of bindu, and the three feet of the Devas and others. 8–9.

Daily, I meditate upon the supreme reality— the pure, absolute *kevala-kumbhaka*— which consists of the *gāyatrī* together with its head and the three channels, situated beyond the two nostrils. (10) Ten repetitions of the *praṇava-gāyatrī*, devoid of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*.
One should perform the filling of the vessel (*kumbha*) through the *suṣumṇā* channel while preceded by the recollection of the mantra.

The rule for breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is recorded as follows: in the lowest [grade] it consists of twelve *mātrās*, in the middling it is considered double that, and in the highest it is declared to be triple. 11–12.
Exhalation (recaka) involves effort, as does inhalation (pūra); however, retention (kumbhaka) is effortless.
Without practice, the scripture is poison; through practice, it becomes nectar.
The best [practice] is said to be threefold, while the middling is likewise twofold.
The noble ones declare that not speaking what is base is called *prāṇāyāma*. It is described as beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with "namas," along with the *mātrā*.
Those who know the *mātrās* understand the *mātrā* to be joined with five and twelve. 14–15.

A practitioner of asceticism should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) using the thumb and the ring finger; likewise, for one who has retired from worldly life, there is indeed the closing of the nostrils.
These five syllables beginning with the letter *va* have been thus proclaimed.
Lam to the self of earth, the fragrance; Ham to the self of space, the flower (17).
Yam to the self of air, the incense; Namah to the self of fire, the lamp; and one should offer the food offering (naivedya) to the self of nectar, the syllable Va (18).
One should perform this mental worship consisting of the five elements;
there is nothing equal to the Siddhāsana, nor anything superior to the Kumbhaka breath-retention.
There is no [posture] equal to the Nanda-dṛṣṭi for the restraint of the vital breath.
Having placed the eyes within and the light without, and having assumed a comfortable posture,
one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) while maintaining equilibrium of the body.
For all living beings indeed, the posture should be comfortable.
Even there, mental [worship] is best; even there, the twice-born is said to be superior. (21) For one dwelling in the forest, the morning twilight alone should be meditated upon;
likewise, having properly closed the nostrils with all five fingers, he should hold them.
One should practice prāṇāyāma very slowly and silently;
having bound the nostrils with the five fingers and restrained the breath, one should draw in and hold the fire (the vital energy), thus practicing prāṇāyāma. 22–23.
Having thus understood breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should bathe Śiva, who consists of consciousness; first, one should properly perform the purely mental retention of breath (kevala-kumbhaka).
Then, one should contemplate the mental worship consisting of the five elements.
One who is endowed with worship and reverence shall obtain the fruit of *prāṇāyāma*.
However, if one performs *prāṇāyāma* without the fivefold worship (*pañcapūjā*), Viśvāmitra has declared that his action is fruitless.
The letter *la*, the letter *bha*, the letter *ya*, the letter *ra*, and the letter *va*—these five phonemes are declared to be the five objects of worship.
*Laṃ* is for the Earth-self, the fragrance; *haṃ* is for the Space-self, the flower.

One should offer incense to the self of air (vāyvātman) and a lamp to the self of fire (agnyātman); one should also present the final offering of food (naivedya) to the self of nectar (amṛtātman), whose essence is the syllable *va*.
One should perform this mental worship, which consists of the five elements.
There is no posture equal to Siddhāsana; there is nothing higher than Kevala-kumbhaka for the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu); and there is no gaze equal to Nandadṛṣṭi.
Having assumed a comfortable posture, one should place the inner light externally while keeping the eyes directed downward.
Having established equilibrium of the body, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For all living beings, a comfortable posture must be adopted; among these, the mental [posture] is best, and among those, the twice-born (brahmin) is said to be superior. 31–32.

At the time of the commencement of the twilight [ritual], the kukkuṭāsana (cock posture) is prescribed; with the arms placed between the knees, one should perform prāṇāyāma. Seated in the candrāsana, which possesses a luster equal to the orb of the moon, [one should practice].
One with perfect vision should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) within the lotus of the heart (34).
In the center of the triangle is the *bindu*, the *praṇava* accompanied by its three parts;
one should daily purify the female and male [principles] according to the procedure for the fivefold worship (35).
One shall obtain the fruit of breath control (prāṇāyāma) by means of the fivefold worship;
one should not fail to perform the fivefold worship, for to do so is fruitless and destructive of the sacred revelation.
When breath control has been attained, one should perform mental worship.
One attains special accomplishment; one should not act fruitlessly.

In the section on the employment of missiles (*astraprayoga*), the power of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is the true strength; one should employ the power of breath-control during the rite of withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*). 37–38.
In both the practice and the conclusion, one should perform the *kumbhaka* breath-retention;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice *prāṇāyāma*.
For he who performs the twilight worship (*sandhyā-vandana*) without *prāṇāyāma*—
One who abandons all dharmas would be a committer of a great sin (mahāpātakin).
Prāṇāyāma is the means for accomplishing the mantras of the Nigamas and Āgamas;
it is accomplished solely through the root-mantras within those Nigama and Āgama mantras. 40–41.
Those who know prāṇāyāma understand it as preceded by mental counting, consisting of syllables such as "sthūla-sthūla" and so forth, and characterized by qualities such as "yukta" and "ayukta";
one should practice prāṇāyāma conjoined with the prāṇa, apāna, and other breaths. 42.

The knowledge of Brahman is the great knowledge, the nectar of seventy million verses on this earth. (43) One should mutter that with the root mantras; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is prescribed, along with the sevenfold recitation of the vyāhṛtis beginning with Bhūḥ according to the universal path. (44)

Likewise, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) by way of reversal; the twice-born should recite the seven Vyāhṛtis along with the Gāyatrī and the Śiras, together with the Śikhā, through both the direct and reverse orders. 45.
The twice-born should chant the prāṇāyāma by means of both the forward and reverse sequences.
Oṃ suvar-bhuvar-bhūr! Hm braṃ taṃ mṛ so ra tī jyopo māṃ oṃ tyādacopra naḥ yo yo dhi hi madhī syava dergo bhayaṃ ṇī re rva tu vi sat tyaṃ sa.
Oṃ paḥ ta oṃ naḥ ja oṃ haḥ ma oṃ haṃ ma oṃ vaḥ su oṃ vaḥ bhūḥ oṃ bhūḥ om.
This king of mantras, the great reality, [is recited] in both direct and reverse order.
One should perform *prāṇāyāma*, which destroys great sins (46).
They know the fruit of *prāṇāyāma* to be for the destruction of great sins, for the removal of great diseases, and for the destruction of suffering and poverty (47).
Reciting the *daśapraṇava-gāyatrī* in both direct and reverse order,
one should properly perform two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
[This purifies] the fault of performing what is forbidden and the great fault of serving a king.

This King of Mantras, when recited in reverse, removes all defects: even the defect caused by one's own actions, the defect of cruel deeds and the like, the defect of harboring the faults of others in one's heart, and the defect of association with the wicked. 49.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, approaching those who should not be approached, eating what should not be eaten, and accepting what should not be accepted—
all these go to destruction through the previously mentioned methods of restraining the breath (vāyurodhana).
What is the use of saying more in this regard? This king of mantras bestows the immeasurable.

A twice-born man who is intent on the application of the Gāyatrī with its ten *praṇavas*, yet fails to perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), becomes one who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇī*).
Through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) performed regularly at the proper time, one certainly dispels all improbable and manifold adverse [results] (53).
[One should recite] the king of mantras sixty-four times, thirty-two times, or half of that.
Half of that is to be known as the lowest; one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) accordingly.
He who performs breath control for a parārdha [of repetitions] of the King of Mantras must undergo a re-consecration (saṃskāra), for his mantra has become fruitless.
O Śūdra, he who restrains for a parārdha of time the sixty-syllable mantra in this very birth shall be born from a non-human womb in his next birth.
He who performs breath control (prāṇāyāma) with a mantra using an unspoken procedure—
To prevent the destruction of his lifespan, poverty may arise in this birth.
(57) If one performs *prāṇāyāma* without the respective root-mantra, one's intentions become fruitless and the deities create obstacles. (58)
The foot that performs the commencement and conclusion is divided into two; [prāṇāyāma] is of three kinds—constant, occasional, and optional—and it becomes fruitless [if performed otherwise].
One should remember one [type of] prāṇāyāma and perform another [type of] recitation; such action is in vain.
The deluded person who performs [the recitation] in two ways obtains no fruit;
[the recitations consist of] half a quarter, a single quarter, two quarters, three quarters, four quarters, five quarters, six quarters, and seven quarters. 60–61.
Prāṇāyāma is prescribed by relying on those respective bases— eight, nine, eighty, and likewise one hundred—
in all the Nigamas and other scriptures, as well as in the Āgamas and so forth. (62)
Having grasped the respective root [mantra], one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Whether it consists of one syllable, two syllables, three syllables, or more,
one should in every way practice breath control with the root mantra.

The Cārvākas, Śaivas, Gāṇeśas, Vaiṣṇavas, and Śāktikas— during their recitation (japa), one should perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma) using the mantras rooted in those [deities]. In the Vedic fire-sacrifice (śrauta-homa), there are ten repetitions, and likewise at evening and morning.
In the Pakṣahoma there are fifteen [oblations], and in the Paśubandha twenty-six;
in the Prāyaścitta there are twenty-four, and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are twenty-one;
wherever negligence occurs, there are thirteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
In both the *aupāsana* fires, there shall be fourteen *prāṇāyāmas* at evening and morning,
and sixteen *prāṇāyāmas* at midday.
One should perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice for the sake of ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Wherever there is a mental resolve, there it is accompanied by duality.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma); beginning from conception (garbhādhāna) up to the end of the ritual placement (ādhāna), it is prescribed for ten ancestors and ten descendants.
They know him as a wicked Brahmin who sells his recitation or the worship of the deities for the sake of another, or who performs acts of hostility for the sake of another;
even if such things are done occasionally through negligence or lack of effort.
One should recite the King of Mantras one hundred times both forward and backward (verses 72);
ten *praṇavas*, the *gāyatrī*, twelve [repetitions], and the restraint of breath;
one should chant the mantra of the garland of letters and perform the recitation for peace (verse 73).
The fault of speaking untruth, the fault of association with the wicked, the fault of performing what is not ordained, the fault of eating bad food and the like,
and the false egoism of "I am"— know these to be the defects of the unworthy twice-born.
The king of mantras, when recited in reverse order, removes all defects.
(74) A twice-born man who performs his ritual bath and twilight prayers regularly at the prescribed times shall destroy all defects.
Through the power of thirty-three koṭis of gods, one will certainly attain right discernment;
[one traverses] a hundred triple-worlds, three hundred triple-worlds.
The foot is the three worlds; the three steps are the three worlds;
the *tāra* is the three worlds; the fourth is the three hundred;
it is the obstruction of the mouth for both the leftward and rightward paths. 76.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Regulation of Prāṇāyāma," in the Viśvāmitra-smṛti.
Now begins the fourth chapter: Mārjana (Sprinkling).

One should step foot by foot, joined with the *praṇava* of joy, and one should cast down eight steps for the destruction of whomever [is targeted]. One who begins with the eight-syllable mantra at each step becomes a slayer of a Brahmin.

One should perform the cleansing at the end of each foot; one shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice. For the sake of whose destruction [this is done], may the waters purify that foot. Having placed one foot upon the ground, one should place the other upon the head.
Having uttered the *praṇava* at the beginning of each quarter-verse (*pāda*), the cleansing (*mārjana*) should be performed at the end of the quarter-verse;

having uttered the *praṇava* at the beginning of each *ṛc*, the cleansing should be performed at the end of the *ṛc*. Having recited the "Āpo hi" hymn nine times twice over, there is a double cleansing for the measure of curd.

Having touched water with the thumb, one should perform the purification (*mārjana*) by means of a foot-measure [of water]. The wise know that purification is of two kinds: with half-mantras or with full mantras;
likewise, it purifies those born of passion, goodness, and darkness, as well as those born of mind, speech, and body.
One should burn these nine—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—with nine [offerings]:
curd, the twice-repeated cleansing mantra, and the four beginning with gold;
this destroys everything, including the group of six beginning with desire and anger.
One should specifically perform the foot-mantra, the arghya-mantra, and the full-mantra; indeed,
for all castes, one should perform the threefold purification by reciting the twenty-four Gāyatrīs according to the number of syllables in each caste.
One should perform the ritual purifications (*mārjana*) according to the path taught in the *Ṛgveda* branch;
such is the characteristic of the purification for the branches of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas.
Now, the sequence of purification for the *Āśvalāyana* branches is stated.

The group of nine beginning with "āpo hiṣṭhā," the two purificatory rites (*dvimārjana*) with "śaṃ no devīḥ," and the three verses beginning with "apsu me" have been declared; thus indeed, the *abliṅga* for the three-verse and nine-verse [sections] is of two kinds. 11–12.
Having uttered the *praṇava* at the beginning of each verse-quarter, the twice-born should perform the ritual cleansing (*mārjana*) at the end of each quarter;
he should likewise perform the cleansings at the beginning of the mantra with the words "ṛtaṃ ca," and then proceed in order from "śanno devī" up to the *Gāyatrī-śiras*.

Having uttered the *praṇava* at the beginning of each *ṛc*, one should perform the ritual purification (*mārjana*). Beginning with the verse "apsume" and ending with "bhūḥ," one should perform three purifications;
there too, having uttered the *praṇava*, one should carry out the purifications.
One should wipe the ground with the *surānta* mantra; there are twenty-four wipes.
Eighteen wipes are prescribed for each quarter-verse (*pāda*), while two wipes are performed with two triple-footed verses (*tripadā*).
In the sixfold rite, the weapons are used in sequence, and the wiping is performed with three *ṛc* verses alone.
One should cast water from the foot downward and upward for its destruction;
twenty-one times on the head and three times one should wipe the ground.
Taking water from the thumb, one should perform the ritual purification (mārjana) at the end of the mantra. 18–18.
One should touch the feet to the ground three times; there should be twenty-one touches on the head.
If one performs this with the eight-syllable mantra at nine places starting from the feet, one becomes a slayer of a Brahmin (atoned).
One should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) at the end of each foot [of the mantra]; one shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).

One should burn away these nine—the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas; those born of mind, speech, and body; and the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—by means of the nine [breaths] joined with the nine *praṇavas* and the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha. (20–21)
One may burn away the sin committed over a year by means of ritual purification (*mārjana*), beginning with the verse "śanno devī" and ending with the six verses beginning with "athā suvaḥ.
Furthermore, these purifications destroy the sins of the group of six internal enemies (*ariṣaḍvarga*).
The cleansing (mārjana) beginning with *apsu me* and ending with *jyok ca sūryam* is the first;
the cleansing beginning with *idam āpaḥ* and ending with *ṛṣabham mehi* is the second;
likewise, the cleansing beginning with *payasvān agne* and ending with *huve* is the third. (23–24)

Beginning with "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ" and extending as far as "antarikṣam atho suvaḥ," the twice-born should perform the ritual cleansing (mārjana) upon the ground according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.
Having thus performed the cleansing, he should practice the Sandhyā-vandana.
Indeed, for one who performs the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) without the characteristic mantra, their sin shall be incalculable and that sprinkling shall be fruitless;
therefore, one should perform the sprinkling according to the scripture with the characteristic mantra. (26–27)
"Being liberated from all sins, no further touch is required once [the body] has been touched"—
thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Method of Sprinkling," in the Viśvāmitra-smṛti.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Description of the Greatness of Offering the Arghya and the Gāyatrī:
A twice-born man should offer three arghyas at the time of the twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana).
In the evening and morning, the procedure should be the same; however, at midday, the rite is performed separately.
One [offering] is at the time of midday, and three each for the evening and morning. Knowing this, one should offer the *arghya* even when the stars have disappeared.
One [arghya] for the destruction of weapons and missiles, one for the long-term destruction of vehicles,
and one for the slaying of the asuras— one should offer these three arghyas in sequence.
After the slaying of the asuras, there is the supreme arghya for atonement (prāyaścitta).
By performing a circumambulation of the earth, one is liberated from all sins.
At the time of the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana), the arghya for expiation is prescribed;
indeed, that foolish twice-born man who offers the arghya with the Gāyatrī alone [is deficient].
He is indeed called a "false Brahmin," excluded from all sacred rites;
for that Vipro who does not know the Brahmāstra is nothing but a Śūdra. All his ritual acts, knowledge, and so forth—all that becomes fruitless.
The seed-mantra of the Gāyatrī is called "Prāṇa" (7).
The body is said to be the "Piṇḍa," while the name itself is the "Kavaca. The word "pada" refers to the mantra of all the limbs; this is the rule for all mantras (8).
The weapon is said to be the rain, and the attainment of Gāyatrī is declared;
having known these six mantras, one should offer the arghya according to the rule.
The Praṇava is always considered the seed-mantra of Gāyatrī.
The Piṇḍa-mantra is the fourth; it is the supreme one known as Gāyatrī.
Nārāyaṇa is the Mūla-mantra, and the Saṃjñā-mantra is always [the same].
"Om āpo jyotiḥ"—this is declared to be the Pada-mantra. 10–11.
"Oṃ tat savituḥ"—this is the Gāyatrī of the heart, O great sage;
for this indeed is the Gāyatrī that bestows liberation upon the wise. They call it the seed-syllable of the Brahmā-missile, and it shall be a shield against the staff of Brahmā.

The *kīlaka* is the "Head of Brahmā," preceded by the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages and other elements. [The syllable] *bhānta* (bha) joined with fire (ra), combined with the sky (ha) and fire (ra), followed by two rams (ma) joined with teeth (da), and thereafter *hālāhala* (ha-la-ha-la). (13–14)
The first syllable is *kha*, preceded by *vāyu* (ya); then another pair of *datta* (da-da) follows.

Then *sarasām akṣaparyāyahāntam* (the end of the synonym for the eye of the waters, i.e., *ha*), followed by *bhūrbhuvaḥ*. After that, *ambaram* (the sky, i.e., *la*) joined with *vāyu* (ya), and then "crush the enemy, crush him" (*ariṃ mardaya mardaya*). 15.
Having uttered "param" twice, one should then utter "etat paraṃ";
thereafter, the three-footed [Gāyatrī] should be employed from the middle mantra of the Gāyatrī.
These three words should be employed; this is remembered as the Brahman-mantra.

For the sake of slaying the Asuras, this Brahmāstra was indeed proclaimed for the twice-born at the time of offering the guest-water (arghya), and during the rites of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā-vandana).
Through the Brahmāstra alone are the goals of ritual action, as well as desire and liberation, attained.
I shall likewise describe the Brahmadaṇḍa, which destroys all weapons and missiles.
Having correctly recited the Gāyatrī joined with the mantra "parorajasi," this indeed becomes the Brahmadaṇḍa, the devourer of all weapons and missiles. 19–20.
For the purpose of destroying all vehicles, I shall describe the Brahmaśīrṣaka weapon.
Having fully recited the Gāyatrī, one should then utter the root mantra.
This indeed is the Brahmaśīrṣaka, which destroys all vehicles.

Having extracted [the breath] from the *ādhāra* and other centers, upon its emergence through the path of the *suṣumṇā*, one should properly perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). That goddess, who pierces the egg of Brahmā, is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. (22–23)
One should assign [the syllables] "Paramātman" according to the direct order (anuloma) for the Gāyatrī;
then, one should assign them in reverse order (pratiloma) for Aghora, Astra, Śārṅga, Nārāca, and Sudarśana. 24.
One *arghya* offering for atonement is prescribed at the time of midday; indeed, two *arghya* offerings are prescribed at midday—this is the truth, O Great Sage. (25)
For the purpose of performing the three-fold *arghya* offering, there is a fourfold expiation (*prāyaścitta*);
this is the sequential rule for the twice-born (*dvijāti*) in the evening and in the morning:
namely, the *Brahmāstra*, the *Brahmadaṇḍa*, and likewise the *Brahmaśīrṣa*.

This has been illustrated for the purpose of the application of the three *arghya* offerings; having recited the triad of mantras beginning with "The Head" (*śīrṣam*) in succession, one should drink the water with cupped palms (*añjali*).
And one should offer the Gāyatrī in reverse order, joined with the seed-syllables and the fourth [syllable] (28); joined with the Head-mantra at each head, one should pour forth the fourfold arghya;
and one should recite the Haṃsa-mantra joined with the Astra, Daṇḍa, and Śiras [mantras] (29).
One should cast a single handful of water as an offering (arghya) for the destruction of weapons, vehicles, and Rakshasas;
this second arghya serves as an expiation and for the slaying of the Asuras.
One should circumambulate the earth clockwise, and thereby one is liberated from all sins.

The Brahmin should perform the *mantra* "haṃsasya" as taught by Brahmādatta (31). Having first uttered the preliminary invocation, he should cast the weapon, staff, and head [of the mantra] toward the face of the enemy, combining the head, staff, and weapon (32).
Having correctly recited the four mantras, one should offer a single *arghya*;
having recited the secondary mantra (*upamantra*) ending with "śiras" and joined with "śreyas," O Great Sage, it is truly stated that one *arghya* should be offered at midday.
The joining of the index finger and the thumb constitutes the Rākṣasī mudrā. Water offered with the Rākṣasī mudrā becomes blood;
if a foolish person should cast it [there], he shall go to the Raurava hell.
By the shadow of the thumb, the water becomes the seal of the deity;
through such a procedure, there shall be the destruction of all the sins of the world.
Having understood this, he who should offer the *arghya* with a perfectly clear mind [attains the fruit]. (36)
Having performed the ritual purification (*mārjana*) with the mantra, "The intermediate space, Svāhā! May the waters purify me from mental sin," he should sip water (*ācamana*).
Then, he should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) nine times using the Vāyavya weapon mantra.
The highest [number of repetitions] for breath control (prāṇāyāma) is nine times; the middling is the number of seasons (six);
and the lowest is said to be three—this is the definition of prāṇāyāma.
Endowed with the power of prāṇāyāma, one should perform the ritual withdrawal (upasaṃhāra). 38–39.

Thereafter, one should perform *prāṇāyāma* with every effort. For this mantra of the venerable Vāyavya-weapon: Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*, Gāyatrī is the *chandas*, the deity is Mahābhūta Vāyu; *yaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and "the creation of the world" is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the employment of the Brahma-weapon and the employment of the Vāyavya-weapon. *Yaṃ* to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*. *Yīṃ* to the two index fingers, *svāhā*. *Yūṃ* to the two middle fingers, *vaṣaṭ*. *Yaiṃ* to the two ring fingers, *hum*. *Yaḥ* to the two little fingers, *vauṣaṭ*. *Yaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands, *phaṭ*.
Thus is the placement of the heart and other limbs; with three verses, the binding of the directions is performed.

I bow to Vāyu, the primordial cause of the universe, whose form is consciousness, who is mounted upon a black antelope, whose meditation is flickering, and who holds arrows, a quiver, a bow, and a sword in his four arms. 40

One should recite three times: *āvāyavyayā vāyavyorvā vāyayā vā hana hana huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Then, having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) nine times while reciting the mantra, and having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should form the resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing Śrī Sūryanārāyaṇa, I shall perform the offering of the *arghya*. Regarding the mantra for the offering of the *arghya*: the Lord Savitṛ is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), Śrī Sūryanārāyaṇa is the deity (*devatā*), the Brahmā-weapon (*brahmāstra*) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the Staff of Brahmā (*brahmadaṇḍa*) is the power (*śakti*), and the Head of Brahmā (*brahmaśīrṣa*) is the pinning-stake (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the offering of the *arghya* for the sake of pleasing Śrī Sūryanārāyaṇa.

*Tatsavitur*—to the Self of Brahmā, *namaḥ* to both thumbs; *vareṇyam*—to the Self of Viṣṇu, *svāhā* to both index fingers; *bhargo devasya*—to the Self of Rudra, *vaṣaṭ* to both middle fingers; *dhīmahi*—to the Self of Īśvara, *hum* to both ring fingers; *dhiyo yo naḥ*—to the Self of Sadāśiva, *vauṣaṭ* to both little fingers; *pracodayāt*—to the Supreme Self, *phaṭ* to both palms and backs of the hands. With these three verses, the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) is performed. The Meditation (*dhyāna*):
Situated in the center of all the arches, established within the mandala, the cause of the true lineage of ten thousand Brahmās. (41)
One should contemplate the Supreme Self as being above and not cast it down, thinking:
"Arise, O Goddess; you must go, and for the sake of returning again.

Taking water with cupped hands, beginning with the *gāyatrī* mantra, one should pour it into the nostril or, having emerged, pour it into the cupped hands and perform the ritual offering (*arghyaprayoga*).

"From every abode, O King, you are the remover from here; know my evil! Whatever has risen today toward the sun, O slayer of Vṛtra, all that is under your control, O Indra"—this is for Āśvalāyana at dawn. For Āpastamba: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose..."—this is for dawn. "You are the embryo; know my evil! [This is for Āśvalāyana]. At dawn: "I invoke the goddess Aditi at midday and at the rising of the sun; O Mitra and Varuṇa, for wealth and for wholeness, for the well-being of our children and progeny, grant us peace."

At midday, for Āpastamba, [the verse] beginning with "He who comes with breath" (*yaḥ prāṇato*) is recited; then follows "Maghaṃ vṛṣabhaṃ na sūryāpanam astāram eṣi sūrya. At evening, for Āpastamba, [the verse] beginning with "He who gives the self" (*ya ātmadā*) is recited.

Having performed *prāṇāyāma* nine times again and having worshipped with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "I shall perform the offering of the fourth *arghya* for the sake of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the slaying of the Asuras. Then, one should offer the fourth *arghya* together with the fourth [syllable], accompanied by the *vāgbhava*, *kāmarāja*, and *śakti* seed-syllables, accompanied by the reverse-order *gāyatrī*, and accompanied by the *śiras* and *śikhā* mantras. Again, having performed *prāṇāyāma* nine times and having worshipped with the five offerings.

Of this mantra for the withdrawal of the divine weapon (astrasaṃhāra), Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), the reverse Gāyatrī is the deity (devatā), *brahma* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *hrīṃ* is the power (śakti), and *hrūṃ* is the pin (kīlaka). Its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of withdrawing the weapon. To the Aghora-weapon, the Śārṅga-bow, the Nārāca-arrow, and the Sudarśana-disc: *hrāṃ dhiyo yo naḥ*; salutation with the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭhābhyām*). To the head, accompanied by the four beginning with Aghora: *svāhā* with the two index fingers (*tarjanībhyām*). Together with the four beginning with Aghora: *hrūṃ*; *vaṣaṭ* with the two middle fingers (*madhyamābhyām*).

Accompanied by the four [mantras] beginning with Aghora: *Hraiṃ Bhargo devasya Oṃ* for the two ring fingers (*anāmikābhyāṃ*), *Hruṃ*. Accompanied by the four [mantras] beginning with Aghora: *Hreṃ Vareṇyaṃ Hrīṃ* for the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ*), *Vauṣaṭ*. Accompanied by the four [mantras] beginning with Aghora: *Tatsavitur Oṃ* for the palms and backs of the hands (*karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ*), *Hruṃ Phaṭ*. Thus is the placement of the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*). *Oṃ Bhūrbhuvaḥ Svaḥ Oṃ* is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). The meditation (*dhyāna*): "I am He; I am the Sun; I am the Light; I am the Light of the Sun; I am Śiva;
I am the Light of the Self; I am the Radiant One; I am the Glory of all lights. (43)

"O Goddess, come and stay; having entered my heart, may the *mudrā* of the goad touch the nostrils with the heart. One should mutter the *gāyatrī* in reverse three times. Having worshipped this Sun, who is Brahman, with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should again place the *vāyavyāstra*. Thus, at the three periods [of the day], the mantra is the same: 'To Aghorāstra, to Śārṅga, to Nārāca, to Sudarśana.'"
One should sequentially perform the nyāsa of the Māyā-ṣaḍdīrgha-gāyatrī in reverse order:
the letter *la*, the letter *ha*, the letter *ya*, the one known as *ra* (repha), and that which is renowned as *va*. One should worship these as being composed of the five elements.
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
Now begins the sixth chapter: the characteristics of the two kinds of japa.

One should perform the recitation of the single-syllabled Brahman, "Om," preceded by ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation, according to one's capacity; this is declared to be the recitation that constitutes a limb of the *sandhyā* rite.
[It should be performed] on a riverbank, at the confluence of rivers, or especially on a mountain peak.
O gods, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī equal to that of Śiva and Viṣṇu.
The characteristics of recitation are twofold: occasional (naimittika) and optional (kāmya). [Next is] the purification of the ground (bhūśuddhi).
One should perform the purification of the ground and the purification of the foundation according to the path of the Guru;
being purified, one should draw the yantra upon the ground with the six syllables beginning with *praṇava*.
This is declared to be called the "foundation" (*ādhāra*); one should then pray to this Earth.
May those beings depart who dwell in the heavens;
may those beings who create obstacles perish by the command of Śiva.
O Earth, you support the worlds; O Goddess, you are supported by Viṣṇu.
And you, O Goddess, hold me; make the seat pure.
Having consecrated it ten times with the six syllables beginning with *praṇava*, one should sprinkle water on the purified ground and draw the supreme yantra.
At the apex of the triangle, one should write the seed-syllable of Fire (Raṃ), and in the center, the syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) with the bindu;
joined with the Tantra, these should be written in sequence at the place of recitation.
One should then draw a square measuring one cubit, which is very firm, soft, and pure.
Seated upon that, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Having performed the purification of the ground with the root mantra, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
carrying out the processes of drying, burning, and floating with the six syllables beginning with the Praṇava.

One hundred and one for the earthly element (pārthiva), two hundred for the syllable *va* (water), three hundred for the seed-syllable of fire (*vahnibīja*), four hundred for the seed-syllable of air (*vāyubīja*),
and five hundred for space (*ākāśa*); this is the sequence for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with *namaḥ*, one should perform one hundred and one repetitions for each [syllable] of increase;
then, one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the five-syllabled mantra to purify the elements of the earth.
Starting from the *mūlādhāra*, one should recite the *gāyatrī* together with the fourth [state].
Having joined [the breath] with the upward-facing [nostril], one should place the Gāyatrī there;
with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the binding of protection for the directions. This destroys minor offenses, diseases, and great sins.
One should contemplate within the belly the evil group of six— lust, anger, and the rest— as black, bearing a sword and a shield, with tawny hair and eyes,
situated upon the island at the end of the syllable *u*, and having the form of a blazing fire. 14–15.
Then, having established the object of desire together with the wind-energy (vāyu-śakti),

one should completely burn it away with the triple flame consisting of the seed-syllable of energy (śakti-bīja). With a concentrated mind, one should reduce it to nothing more than its remaining radiance, like camphor.

Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ—one should perform drying. Oṃ iṃ namaḥ—having performed burning with the seed-syllable of fire. Oṃ vaṃ namaḥ—having performed flooding with the seed-syllable of nectar, one should discard the limbs and so forth, measuring ninety-six finger-breadths, by means of "laṃ namaḥ. Oṃ haṃ namaḥ—with the seed-syllable of space, one should establish the appearance of all perceptions. From the feet up to the knees is designated as the earth-maṇḍala; from the knees up to the hips is designated as the water-maṇḍala. 17.
From the throat down to the waist is known as the fire-maṇḍala;
from the heart up to the ears is known as the air-maṇḍala;
and from the ears up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) is known as the space-maṇḍala. 18.
This purification of that which consists of the five elements has been proclaimed.
[One should perform it] two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths from the penis,
using either the root-mantra of Suṣumnā or the four-syllabled mantra.

Having meditated upon a verse with the radiance of shimmering gold within that creeper of lightning, one should lead the *kulakuṇḍalinī* through the sequence of piercing the six-petaled centers of the *suṣumnā* to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). There, one should cause her to dissolve into Śiva—the Supreme Self in the form of the syllable *Oṃ*—who is the complete *gāyatrī* situated in the center of the thousand-petaled lotus of the *kula*. [This is done] by means of the noose, goad, and hook, using the seed-syllables beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.

One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) one hundred and eight times in this manner; then one should perform the five-fold worship of oneself in the form of the *haṃsa*. With the realization of "I am He" (*so'ham*), one should unite [the self] from the sky into the solar orb.
Having drawn forth the Goddess, one should sustain her and perform the bathing of the vital breaths;

then, with the two syllables "Haṃsa," one should worship the life-force and consciousness residing in the heart through the state of "So 'ham" (I am He), according to the procedure of the fivefold worship. 23. So 'ham. Bhāvena. Saṃpūjya. Pañcapūjānusārataḥ.
One should perform *prāṇāyāma* according to the stated number and method.
For the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are declared to be the seers (*ṛṣis*), and the three Vedas are its meters (*chandāṃsi*).

The deity is the vital power (prāṇa-śakti), the seed-syllable is the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka) is the triad beginning with the fetter (pāśa); these are to be employed in the locus of the vital breath. Likewise, there is the king of seed-syllables, the seed of the fetter, consciousness, and the goad (aṅkuśa).

Then, following that, one should recite the fifty-syllable mantra of the two *haṃsas*, sequentially encapsulated by *nādas*, by the consonant groups beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*, and by the two acts of salutation (*natī*). 27.
One should perform the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs using the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*).

Reciting the *praṇava*, the power of breath (*prāṇaśakti*), the noose (*pāśa*), illusion (*māyā*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), joined with the third vowel and pronouncing the consonants from *ya* to *ha*, [one should perform the assignment]. 28–29.
One should recite "mama prāṇāḥ" and so forth, ending with the consort of fire (svāhā); then, while reciting the triad beginning with *pāśa*, the power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*), and the *tāra* (oṃ),
one should perform the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*) after chanting this mantra once.
Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) on the hands and touched the heart according to the command of the Guru,
one should properly recite this mantra ten times according to the prescribed rule. 31
One should recite the *prāṇasūkta* prescribed in one's own branch of the Veda three times, joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and end; then,
one should perform *prāṇāyāma* during the restraint of the microcosm (*piṇḍa*) and the macrocosm (*brahmāṇḍa*).

One should perform the visualization of the seat (*āsana*) as extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*, resembling a stalk made of coral and ruby, unbroken and blazing, filled with wonder, most effective at dispelling the darkness of all sins, consisting of light, three-footed, yet possessing the fourth state (*turya*), its luminous nature formed by the mass of splendor following the king of mantras; it serves as the seat for the body that touches as far as the breath.
The letter *Ha* is to be known as the *praṇava*, and likewise the letter *Sa* as *prakṛti*. One should perform *prāṇāyāma* in sequence with the letters of the *Mātṛkā*.

One should perform the purification of the hands with [the syllables] joined with the six long vowels (34). Having assigned the group of six beginning with the seer (*ṛṣi*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs.
First, one should place the seer on the head; the meter (*chandas*) is said to be placed on the mouth (35).
Having placed the deity in the heart, the seed-syllable is said to be in the navel;
one should place the Śakti in the foundation (ādhāra) and the kīlaka at the feet. 36.
Brahmā is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is said to be the metre (chandas).

The deity is the external *mātṛkā*, while the consonants (*hal*) are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the vowels (*svara*) are declared to be the powers (*śakti*). "Salutation" (*namaḥ*) is said to be the *kīlaka*.
[This is done] by enclosing [the mantra] with pairs of letters beginning with the letter *ha*.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs using the letters beginning with *ka*, conjoined with the principles (*tattva*).
One should perform the binding with the three worlds, meditate, and display the *yonimudrā*.
[One should meditate on her] whose slender body is fashioned from the fifteen syllables, who has a third eye on her forehead, and who is beautiful like the digits of the full moon.
Worship Varṇeśvarī, who is as fair as jasmine and the moon, holding in her hands a mudrā, a rosary, a jewel, and a book.

(40) One should place the vowels at the end of the hair, on the face, on the two eyes, on the two ears, on the two nostrils, on the two lips, on the two rows of teeth, and on the seat of the head. (41)
One should place the letters beginning with *ya* in the joints of the arms and feet, at the pair of their toes, on the back, within the navel,
and likewise in the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Then, one should perform the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (*antarmātṛkā-nyāsa*) according to the path prescribed by the rules.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the three *tāras*.
The seer, meter, deity, seed-syllable, power, and pin;
Brahmā, the script, and the Gāyatrī—thereafter, the internal *mātṛkā* is prescribed.
Having understood that the triad consisting of the Vāgbhava, Śakti, and Śrī Bījas, as well as the three Tāras, is thus proclaimed, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should perform the karanyāsa and the hṛdinyāsa with the three Tāras.

Having performed the binding of the directions with the three worlds through both direct and reverse order, and having meditated upon it, one should then display the Great Yoni Mudrā. 46. Mudrā! [Thus it is said.]
Through fifty-fold births from his own body, by means of various kinds of actions (karma),
47 By means of many meaningful words, phrases, and syllables, and by well-endowed limbs,
this [work] is characterized by infinite fruits of intentional mental actions for those who are not yet awakened. 48
"Even though you are the universal self of consciousness, you manifest as 'I, I' within the matrix (mātṛkā).
Having spoken thus, one should arrange the two mātṛkās according to the prescribed method.
Then, one should display the ten mudrās through the various distinctions such as invocation (āvāhana) and the rest.
One should offer oblations of sacrificial food mixed with ghee during the invocation and the seating [of the deity];
or else, one may perform the daily rite even with rice grains.
Having performed the "three unknowns" (anājñāta), one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times.
It is prescribed that [the mantra] with the Praṇava at the beginning, end, and middle should be recited at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice;
one should mutter these twenty-four syllables during the Pārāyaṇa.
In both the Japa and the Pārāyaṇa, it should be performed joined together and then separately in sequence.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs joined with the four syllables.
Excluding the fourth quarter, one should perform the placement from beginning to end along with the *praṇavas*.
Having uttered the three *vyāhṛtis* and the four-syllabled *Gāyatrī*, [one should proceed]. 53–54.
Having again uttered the *vyāhṛtis*, one should perform the ritual assignment (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs;
with each foot and each half-verse enclosed by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), the six-footed [mantra] becomes three-footed through its application in the hand and limb assignments. 55.

The four syllables beginning with the thumb [of the fingers] are in direct order (anuloma), and the four syllables beginning with the heart are likewise in reverse order (viloma). However, if one were to place them in a reversed sequence without these four syllables, [it would be incorrect]. 56–57.
He meets with misfortune; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
