With the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, impelling it for the sake of illumination within the body consisting of ninety-six constituents. 58.
Then one should demonstrate the mantra-bonding of the directions (*digbandha*) by means of the three worlds:
Haṃsasiṃhāsana, Vahni, Viśvayoni, as well as Khecarī, Kuṇḍalīkuṇḍa, and the seal of the seven *vyāhṛtis*. 59–60.
The *sumukha* (well-faced), the *saṃpuṭa* (joined-palms), the *vitata* (extended), and likewise the *vistṛta* (spread-out);
the two-faced, the three-faced, and likewise the four- and five-faced;
the six-faced, the downward-facing (*adhomukha*), and likewise the all-pervading *añjali* (clasped-hands) gesture.
The cart, the noose of Yama, the entwined [posture] facing forward and backward;
the hanging, the fist, as well as the fish, the tortoise, and the boar;
the lion-attack, the great-attack, the mallet, and likewise the sprout.
These are the twenty-four mudrās; [the verse] "gāyatrī supratiṣṭhitā" refers to the mudrās.
If one does not know the mudrās, the Gāyatrī becomes fruitless.
(64) I worship [her] through meditation with faces possessing the luster of pearls, coral, gold, sapphire, and white.
Having uttered the *tāra* (om), the fourth foot [of the Gāyatrī], the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the power (*śakti*), and the pin (*kīlaka*),
one should place the three sets of three— the seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth— in their respective order.
This is applied for the grace of the Goddess through the complete Gāyatrī.

One should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs, beginning with the seed-syllables, powers, and stakes, in both direct and reverse order, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ). Then, one should perform the binding of the directions (digbandhana) using the three worlds [syllables] ending with the Praṇava.

I perpetually bow to that sixth face of Pātāla, which is meditation (dhyāna), worshipped by gods and asuras, resembling the dawn, honored by the sun, the hosts of stars, and by flowers such as the punnāga, ambuja, nāga, and bakula, as well as by incense and other offerings; it is eternally the sustainer of all and the source of all radiance, comparable to Rudra at the fire of time (kālāgnirudra), and the agent of universal dissolution.
The crest-source (śikhāyoni), the great yogi, and the deity on the crown of the head;
the linga-mudrā, the mahāmudrā, and the añjali—these are the eight mudrās.
At the times of morning and midday, one should perform the fourth quarter [of the rite] ten times over.

In the evening, one should perform the recitation (japa) together with the four limbs. At the conclusion of the recitation, one should contemplate the eight [mudrās]: Surabhi, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Yoni, Śaṅkha, Paṅkaja, Liṅga, and Nirvāṇa-mudrā. 69–70.

"In the yoga [practice], however, according to the procedure stated in the Ṛgveda branch, it is done in reverse order; but in the case of recitation without a formal ritual application, the *anuloma* (direct) order does not exist. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Prescription of Various Ritual Applications," in the Viśvāmitra-smṛti.
Now begins the seventh chapter:
the description of the rules for the ritual attendance (upasthāna).
The ritual attendance.
Now, therefore, I shall explain in due order the procedure for attendance according to the ritual prescribed in the Ṛgveda branch, beginning with the verse "jātavedase" (1),
to be recited at both morning and evening according to the stated method.
At midday, there is a separate *sandhyā* rite;
at that time, the twice-born, while gazing at the sun— the Jātavedas— should perform the worship of Durgā by reciting the thousand-verse goddess (*sahasra-paramā*) while standing in water.
Having observed the sun at the end of the day, one should offer four *arghya* oblations;
until the stars appear, one should likewise mutter these four-footed verses.
One should mutter these *ṛc*s—beginning with "O Jātavedas"—both in the morning and in the evening.
At the edge of the water, one should perform the ritual worship according to the rules with a concentrated mind;
having uttered the Haṃsa-mantra and reciting the three-footed Gāyatrī,
one should offer a single *arghya* at midday for those who are masters of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
The expiation and the second *arghya* are for the sake of slaying the Asuras;
indeed, at midday, there are two *arghyas* for all [the deities] in this very same manner. After the offering of the *arghya*, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī* as before.

When the sun has turned back [from its southern course], one should perform the ritual worship (upasthāna) with the mantra "ud u tyam," according to the sequence of rules prescribed in the Ṛgveda branch;
at midday, the meditation on the sun should be performed as it is in the morning and evening.

Having performed the midday *saṃdhyā* ritual, one should recite [the mantra] until the end of the *āvartana*, which lasts for thirteen *ghaṭikās*; thereafter follows the *upasthāna*. If one performs the *upasthāna* without the daily recitation (*jāpya*), [it is ineffective].
Having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī preceded by all the solar mantras,
one should gaze at the sun until it sets and perform the ritual of worship (upasthāna).
Having recited [the mantra] at both sunrise and sunset, one should perform the worship of Durgā.
At midday and at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the worship of the Sun (sūryopasthāna),
as prescribed in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra for those belonging to the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedic schools.
At the end of both the recitation and the worship, one should perform the fivefold solar worship (pañcārcana).
Having observed the reflection appearing at the end of the radiance as it rises, one should say that [the mantra] has been "fully risen" (*kṛtodita*).
Regarding the mantra, the verses of the sages (*ārṣa*) and so forth should be worshipped by those of the *Yajurveda* according to the recensions of other branches (*śākhāntara*).
Through the repetition (*japa*) of three lines, there is a threefold merit; the repetition of four lines yields a tenth part [of that merit].
If one performs recitation (japa) without the fourth foot [of the Gāyatrī], it shall be fruitless.

Having performed the *carṣaṇi-mantra* of Mitra according to the sequence of Yājurvedic worship, one should perform the ritual attendance upon the Sun (sūryopasthāna) with the Gāyatrī at the conclusion of the morning recitation. 15–16.

With the mantra beginning with "ā satyena," according to the prescribed rule for the six verses, one should meditate upon the Sun at midday; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should proceed according to the ritual sequence.
In the evening, two ghaṭīs after the setting of the Sun, one should cease from the ritual action.
Reciting the mantra of the captivating Goddess until the stars appear,
one should, upon observing the sun eclipsed, perform the ritual of worship to the directions and recite the Vāruṇa hymn as well as the mantra beginning with "imaṃ me. 18–19.
Having recited the *Priyāsūkta*, one should meditate upon the four-footed Goddess;
having worshipped her with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should [worship] Gāyatrī together with the Fourth (*turyā*).
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual of Prostration" (*upasthāna*), in the *Viśvāmitrasmṛti*.
Now begins the eighth chapter:
the description of the rules for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and other offerings to the gods.

I shall now describe the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*) and other rites according to the rules prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. Furthermore, one should avoid *kōdrava*, *māsu* beans, *māṣa* beans, *masūra* lentils, those produced from *kulattha*, salt, and pungent vegetables during the *vaiśvadeva* offering.

Then, for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one should daily and without weariness provide wild rice, bamboo-seed grain, wheat, and rice, as well as bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, along with curd, milk, and ghee. 2–3.
When a householder begins the rite of Vaiśvadeva,
the twice-born one, having taken the cooked food prepared in the home along with curd, milk, and ghee,
sits upon his seat of recitation for his own purpose before cooking for all others.
For whoever should offer that [oblation] into the fire preceded by the Gāyatrī mantra—
offering the oblation to Sūrya by day and to Agni by night— and should offer one oblation to Prajāpati for both, (5–6).
Having offered oblations with the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the mantras belonging to one's own Vedic school,
one who desires long life should present a bali-offering to the spirits day and night, carrying the bali in the shape of a ladle.
For the purpose of destroying death and disease, one should offer an oblation (bali) in human form.
In rites for specific desires and in speech, one should offer the oblation like an anthill.
[This brings] long life, health, sovereignty, sons, grandsons, and cattle.
He who desires liberation should offer a circular *bali* sacrifice;
for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, he should also offer a *bali* with a fan.
Among these five, O Brahmins, this fourth one is the most important.
The first [garment] should be worn as the *upavīta*, the second as the *nivītika*,
and the third is prescribed for the *pitṛmedha* and the *vaiśvadeva* rites.
One should especially prepare cooked food combined with rice and water.
One should not cook rice in boiling water; however,
if one should cook rice in boiling water,
that rice should be known as poison, equal to the eating of cow-flesh.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat and has been kept for a long time;

likewise, wheat and barley, even when not mixed with fat, may be eaten if they have been mixed with cow's milk, provided ghee is added during cooking and the food is carefully removed from the fire once cooked. 14–15.
Having poured ghee over it, one should especially divide the portions for the sake of sacrifice,
for the worship of the gods, for the sake of Brahmins, and for the ritual offering (bali). One should not prepare separate cooking, particularly for the Vaiśvadeva rite.

O best of the twice-born, one should prepare the sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) with kuśa grass, dividing it into five portions. Having sprinkled those portions with clarified butter first and then with the oblation (huta), one should perform the fivefold worship followed by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having proclaimed the place and the time, one should then perform the ritual action;
then, with each of the first six mantras, one should offer oblations with the hand.
Having made the mind steady and fixed, one should personally cook [the offering] with the fire of knowledge.
He who is devoted to his own duty and cooks for himself alone is called a *svayaṃpākī*.
One should never abandon the *vaiśvadeva* offering, whether it be performed without mantras or with mantras;
by performing the *vaiśvadeva*, one is not defiled by the faults of food. (20–21)
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules in the morning and at midday,

and likewise in the evening. Having divided the sacrificial rice (haviṣya-taṇḍula) into two portions every day, one should cook it and offer the oblation as a dedication to the deity after performing the homa.
He who eats after having offered oblations and given gifts is called a *svayaṃpākī* (one who cooks for himself).
To remove the five slaughterhouses [of the body], one should offer the sacrificial oblation as an expiation;
there is no other purifier born of that [fire] than this, for if it is absent, there is impurity.
One should never perform two separate Vaiśvadeva fire-offerings on one side;
however, he who does so should observe a fast and perform the rite again after rising on the following day and bathing according to the prescribed rules. 25.

One should perform the cooking according to the prescribed rule and perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the six-syllable mantra. One should offer oblations preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava), using the words "bhūḥ bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," one hundred and eight times, according to the procedure stated in one's own Sūtra.
Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite in due order according to the rules;
thereafter, the offering of bali should be performed, and the expiation (prāyaścitta) is prescribed.
When both types of birth-impurity (sūtaka) have occurred simultaneously, one should suspend the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
One should perform the recitation of the *Pārāyaṇa*, avoiding both loud and whispered tones.
When the eleventh day has arrived, one should prepare separate food and perform the *Vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and the *Bali* offering according to the prescribed rules.

In a *śrāddha* for a deceased person, one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* offering with a separate cooking; however, on the anniversary of death (*kṣaya*), on the new moon (*darśa*), and during the fortnightly rites (*pakṣa*), a single cooking is prescribed.
If, in a *śrāddha* for a deceased person, a separate cooking is performed without [the *vaiśvadeva*], [it is defective].

The Rākṣasas accept [the offering], and the one who performs the cooking falls downward. (32) Herein is the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva section: it shall consist of fourteen ghaṭikās beginning from sunrise. (33)
There should be fifteen ghaṭikās, then sixteen,
after that seventeen are proclaimed, and eighteen are recorded thereafter.
At the conclusion of the confluence, one should perform the Brahma-yajña preceded by a ritual bath.
The midday twilight rite, the libation (tarpaṇa), and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice— these are the sequence. At the midday time, when the sun is in its southern course,
one should perform the Vaiśvadeva before the actual midday hour.
At the end of midday, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva after nine ghaṭikās have passed;
when the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), one should perform the Vaiśvadeva [at that time]. However, from fourteen ghaṭikās until sunrise, [it may also be performed].
Having performed the libation for others, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite (verse 38).
According to the procedure known as the three seasons (*ṛtutraya*), on both the southern and northern paths,
beginning from sunrise and after eight *ghaṭikās* (verse 39).
At the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa), one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite according to the prescribed rule.
The determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva of the yogins is now stated:
one should not offer the oblation in the middle watch of the night, nor should one let two watches pass by.
This is declared to be the time for the Vaiśvadeva rite of yogis;
however, the yogi who performs it otherwise becomes fallen.
This is declared to be the primary rule for the Vaiśvadeva of yogis.

Having set aside the *balikriyā*, one should perform the six daily offerings (*nitya-ṣaḍāhuti*); one should not perform an intermediate *balikriyā*, for it is traditionally taught that there is only one external offering (*bāhya-bali*).
According to the *Kauṣātaki-smṛti*, one should offer food with the first six [mantras].
Therefore, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as prescribed in the Vedas according to the rules.
By performing the Vaiśvadeva, a mendicant removes the fault incurred by not doing it;
however, the Vaiśvadeva does not remove the fault of not giving alms for a mendicant.
If a mendicant arrives seeking alms when the Vaiśvadeva offering has not yet been performed,
one should set aside a portion for the Vaiśvadeva and, having given him alms, dismiss him;
even if one has carried away a load of wood or a hundred jars of clarified butter.
The fire sacrifice of one whose guest has departed with unfulfilled hopes is useless.
He from whose house guests arrive from afar and are well-satisfied is called a true householder; all others are merely guardians of their homes.
Any cooking performed without the Vaiśvadeva rite is called *sapratyanāmaka*; if a Brāhmaṇa eats such food, he becomes fallen immediately.
A mendicant (*bhikṣu*), however, is capable of removing the fault arising from the omission of the Vaiśvadeva.
One should avoid sandals, a yogic belt, a sacred thread, and a variegated woolen blanket;

likewise, one should avoid the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā* during the Vaiśvadeva rite, as well as silver on the forefinger. One whose father is still living should perform the six daily oblations.
If one is commanded by his father, he may perform the Vaiśvadeva rite; however, in the case of unrefined food, offerings at fixed shrines, and in houses,
he who performs it without the utterance of "svāhā" becomes a Brahmarākṣasa.

One should offer sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) to the gods, including those of the moving and non-moving worlds (carācarādi-devānām). Having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite for the sake of removing the five slaughter-houses (pañcasūnā),
one should offer oblations as an expiation (prāyaścitta) for the removal of the five slaughter-houses.
One should then offer that food as an oblation (naivedya) to the deities;

for by means of this offering to the Viśvedevas, they perform the offering of the sacrificial oblation (havis) to the twice-born gods. Those who do so [otherwise] are great sinners, and that oblation becomes swarming with worms.
Food prepared by a widow, a barren woman, or one who has made a widow; likewise that of a deaf person or a mute, and that of a pregnant woman whose pregnancy is fruitless—these should never be eaten.
Having recognized the five kinds of widows, one should diligently avoid them. 56–57.
If a girl is set on fire in a cremation ground upon a funeral pyre, like a desired piece of wood, she is called a *vīra* by the wise;
she is a widow of Rohiṇī, and she is designated as a *raṇḍā*. 58.1–2.
A maiden who is ten years old and yet unfortunate is so described; however, she who has passed beyond her menses becomes a widow, and that woman who is childless is called a *raṇḍā*. 59–60.
With various efforts and through diverse means, one should avoid the cooking of a *raṇḍā* (an abandoned woman):
namely, a *vīra-raṇḍā*, a *kuṇḍa-raṇḍā*, a woman whose son is a child, or one who has no son at all.
One must not eat the food cooked by them; if one does eat it, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
A widow who does not bathe, a fierce woman, one who eats cooked food during the month of impurity after childbirth—
these five types of cooked food a Brahmin should avoid, as should the service of such a person. For if he prepares the food with effort and then eats it, it is indeed poison.
One should abandon the food cooked by a widow during the Vaiśvadeva rite, for it is a great sin;
one should not eat food that has not been offered in sacrifice, as he considers it to be non-offering.
The food cooked by a widow is cruel poison, and likewise, food that has not been offered in sacrifice is poison.
That food joined with the two-fold machine is the Kālakūṭa poison;
one should diligently avoid the cooking of a widow through various means.
If such food is obtained through negligence, fourteen rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) must be performed.

One should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering, which is the first portion of the oblation for the King of Mantras, by means of the *kumbhaka* breath-retention, preceded by ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation;
having done so, one should perform the *śrāddha* and carry out the obligatory and occasional rites.

Having performed the Vaiśvadeva rite prior to the *agnaukaraṇa* (the offering into the fire) of the *śrāddha*, one should then perform the *agnaukaraṇa*; otherwise, one is a destroyer of the *śrāddha*.
For he who performs the *śrāddha* rite without the Vaiśvadeva [is likewise at fault].
That *śrāddha* becomes in vain, and he shall go to the Raurava hell;
therefore, having diligently cooked the food for the daily and occasional *śrāddhas*,
one should then perform the *homa* and subsequently feed the Brahmins.
One should perform the fire-offering preceded by the Vaiśvadeva rite;
that oblation shall be an offering unto Brahman, and what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
Likewise, there is an oblation for the gods, the ancestors, and the sages. (71–72)
If food is first offered into the mouth of the fire, it leads to satisfaction; otherwise, it is not so.

He who offers food in the rites for the gods and ancestors without having first made an oblation into the fire—his food becomes that of the clan-demons (gotrapa), and his śrāddha is in vain; of this there is no doubt.

In the daily *śrāddha*, in the *gayā-śrāddha*, and likewise in the *tīrtha-śrāddha*, one should first perform the *vaiśvadeva* offering; thereafter, one should perform the *śrāddha*. Having first offered with the utterance of "svāhā," one should then offer with the utterance of "svadhā."
Having thus performed the three oblations, one should then perform the śrāddha;
regarding the Vaiśvadeva,
one should offer sacrificial food mixed with ghee into the fire in equal portions throughout the three watches of the night.
Two plus two makes four; this is known as the "pair," beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and joined with each respective mantra (76).
Accompanied by the six flavors and consisting of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), as well as rice mixed with ghee, a Brāhmaṇa should always perform this Vaiśvadeva rite without weariness (77).
If one performs the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice while setting aside food intended for another,
he incurs the curse of the gods and will certainly become impoverished.
(78) [This applies even to] royal food that is well-cooked, seasoned with flavors, and mixed with ghee.

Knowing that it was intended as an oblation, the thirty gods were well-pleased. On the two festival days, at the conjunction [of the moon], having prepared a meal with great care for the Vaiśvadeva rite at the conclusion of the Śrāddha, they departed. (79–80)
Having offered oblations, having given gifts, and having eaten, a twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
for at the time of the Śrāddha, sacrificial food must be offered in turn by the twice-born to the gods, the sages, and especially to the ancestors.
A single cooking is prescribed for the sake of pleasing the gods, sages, and ancestors (82).
A separate cooking must not be performed; if it were done, one would become fallen.
Furthermore, he who performs the food offering (*naivedya*) without first preparing the meal will become swarming with worms (83).
"Having performed the *homa* with diligence, one should arrange the *vaiśvadeva* offering.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled the Section on the *Vaiśvadeva*, in the *Viśvāmitra-smṛti*.
